facts.text: Before the American Revolution, there were 13 British colonies along the east coast of North America where about 2.4 million colonists lived.
The land where the colonies were built had belonged to many different indigenous nations for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.
The colonists had to follow rules made by the King of England and the British Parliament, even though they lived far away across the ocean.
Britain made colonists pay new taxes, like the Stamp Act of 1765, to help pay for earlier wars, but the colonists had no say in making these laws.
In 1770, British soldiers shot and killed five colonists in Boston. Crispus Attucks, a Black man, was among the first to die for American freedom.
In the Boston Tea Party of 1773, colonists dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor to protest unfair taxes on tea.
On July 4, 1776, the Continental Congress approved the Declaration of Independence, announcing that the colonies were free from Britain.
Thomas Jefferson was the main writer, but a committee of five people including Benjamin Franklin and John Adams helped create the Declaration.
The Declaration says that all people are created equal with rights to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
The first battles of the Revolution were fought at Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts, on April 19, 1775.
George Washington led the Continental Army through the whole war, including a famous surprise crossing of the icy Delaware River on Christmas night 1776.
France and Spain helped the American colonies fight against Britain by sending soldiers, ships, and supplies.
The war ended in 1783 when Britain signed the Treaty of Paris and recognized American independence.
When the Declaration said all men are created equal, it did not include enslaved people, women, or indigenous peoples. About 500,000 people were enslaved in the colonies.
About 20,000 enslaved African Americans joined the British side after Lord Dunmore promised freedom to those who escaped and fought for Britain.
About 9,000 Black soldiers fought on the American side, and roughly one out of every five soldiers in the northern Continental Army was Black.
Phillis Wheatley, an enslaved woman in Boston, became a famous poet who wrote about liberty and even sent a poem to General George Washington.
The powerful Iroquois Confederacy (Six Nations) in New York had governed themselves with their own laws and leaders long before Europeans arrived.
The Revolution split the Iroquois Confederacy: the Oneida and Tuscarora sided with the colonists, while the Mohawk, Seneca, Onondaga, and Cayuga sided with Britain.
After the war, many indigenous peoples lost their homelands as the new United States expanded westward, even though they had lived on these lands for thousands of years.
Americans celebrate the Fourth of July every year with fireworks, parades, barbecues, and picnics to remember the day the country declared its independence.
The Liberty Bell in Philadelphia is a famous symbol of American freedom that was rung to celebrate the first public reading of the Declaration of Independence.
Independence Hall in Philadelphia is where both the Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were signed, and people visit it from all over the world.
